extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners, patent office management, patent practitioners and other IP stakeholders (public commenters)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and metrics used by the USPTO to set and evaluate examiner production goals, define examining time, allocate counts/production units, and model how examination time affects pendency, workload, and quality. Also solicits public input on time/quality tradeoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Model (simulation tool)
rubrics_metrics.description: Simulation tool that predicts pendency, workload and output.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to plan hiring and other factors to ensure pendency goals are met and to project revenue and costs. Key inputs include projected filings, examiner attrition, management decisions on hiring, overtime and special programs, and quality investments such as training and additional examining time. Predicted outputs include future staffing levels, total production, application inventories, and pendency. Individual examiner production goals are critical determinants of how inputs relate to outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner Performance Appraisal Plan (weighted elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiner performance is rated on: 35% Productivity; 35% Quality; 20% Docket Management; 10% Stakeholder Interaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The overall annual performance rating is a weighted average of Production, Docket Management, Quality, and Stakeholder Interaction. Production is measured by actual Production Units achieved relative to the examiner’s production goal. The plan provides feedback mechanisms to improve performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production Unit (PU) definition and counts distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: A Production Unit (PU) equals 2 counts. Counts are awarded for prosecution events (e.g., 1st action on merits: 1.25 counts; final rejection: 0.25 counts; disposal—allowance, appeal, or abandonment: 0.50 counts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each serial new (non-RCE) application carries 1 PU (2.0 counts), with fractions awarded for each major office action type. The distribution is structured to incentivize a thorough first action by awarding most of the PU at first action and less for follow-on actions. No credit is given for rework (e.g., 2nd non-final). In most cases, RCEs carry a fraction of a PU (e.g., 1.75 counts) and the credit for a first action is reduced correspondingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production goal calculation formula
rubrics_metrics.description: Number of Examining Hours x Seniority Factor / Technology Complexity = Number of PUs needed for 100% of goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The production goal for each examiner is calculated from the number of Examining Hours worked in the evaluation period and quantitative values assigned to examiner seniority and technology complexity. Performance under the Production element is assessed by comparing actual PUs achieved to the expected PUs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examining Hours (inclusions and exclusions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examining Hours include all major examination activities (reviewing the application; analyzing the claims; searching prior art; considering prior art including IDS; consulting colleagues; writing office actions; addressing applicant responses; administrative activities like reading/responding to email).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examining Hours are a subset of an examiner’s compensated time—generally activities that directly relate to examination and generation of a production unit. Excluded are leave and holidays, training, staff meetings, and programs where examiners receive additional time (e.g., AFCP 2.0, QPIDS).

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology Complexity (hours per PU and adjustment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Technology Complexity designates a baseline amount of time per application (unadjusted expectancies range ~13.8 to 31.6 hours/PU for utility applications). Examples: fishing lures 16.6 hours/PU; immunotherapy 25.9 hours/PU; satellite communication 27.7 hours/PU.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each application is classified with an associated unadjusted expectancy based on technology. These unadjusted expectancies are adjusted based on the examiner’s seniority and feed into the production goal calculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seniority Factor adjustment
rubrics_metrics.description: A numeric seniority factor multiplies examining hours; as examiner seniority (GS level) increases, the seniority factor increases (more production expected). Example factors used in slides: GS-7 = 0.7, GS-12 = 1.0, GS-14 = 1.35.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seniority factor quantitatively adjusts expected production to reflect examiner experience; it is one of the multiplicative terms in the production goal formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production achievement (% completion) calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: Achievement percentage = actual PUs completed / expected PUs. Example: convert actual counts to PUs, then divide by expected PUs (e.g., 6.25 actual PUs / 5.9 expected PUs = 107%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counts from actions are converted to PUs (2 counts = 1 PU) and compared to the expected PUs for the pay period to determine percent achievement toward the production goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent examination tasks (time-consuming activities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent examination comprises a variety of tasks: analyze new application; perform initial search; prepare initial first action; consider IDS; prepare subsequent actions; perform subsequent search; prepare after-final response; communications to Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each task consumes a greater or lesser share, on average, of the total time required to examine an application. Time allotments and expected activity composition should reflect these task types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of changing examination time on pendency
rubrics_metrics.description: Examination time per application (decreased/increased) affects projected pendency according to the Patent Model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pendency can be maintained at baseline by adjusting key inputs such as hiring and other management decisions. The model demonstrates tradeoffs between time per application and resources required (e.g., hiring, overtime).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality in complex technologies (request for comment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Question: Do you perceive a difference in the quality of examination performed in complex technologies compared to less complex technologies? If yes, which do you perceive as higher quality and why? In what aspect(s) is the quality of examination higher?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the USPTO’s public request for comment to inform how examination time and quality considerations should vary across technology complexity; responses should explain perceived quality differences and aspects where quality differs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimating time for prosecution (request for comment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Question: What factors do you consider when estimating the amount of time needed to take various steps in prosecution (e.g., preparing responses, preparing for interviews)? How do those factors vary among technology areas?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USPTO requests specifics about factors used by practitioners to estimate prosecution time so the agency can refine time allotments and expectancies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complexity of prosecution over time (request for comment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Question: Are the applications you prosecute more or less complex than in the past (e.g., 10 years ago)? What factors contribute to increases or decreases in complexity? Has this affected the amount of time to prosecute and the quality of examination? If so, by how much and how?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solicits empirical or anecdotal evidence on trends in complexity, time impacts, and quality effects to inform recalibration of examination time expectancies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination activities allocation to improve quality (request for comment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Question: To increase the quality of examination, should increased time be designated for specific activities (e.g., interviews) or left to examiner discretion? What activities would you prioritize and allocate more time to?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asks stakeholders to identify concrete activities that would benefit from more assigned time versus leave decisions to examiner judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of portions of Office actions (request for comment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Question: Are there any portions of Office actions which you feel do not add value or quality to the examination? If yes, what are they?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seeks identification of low-value portions of office actions that could be reduced to reallocate examiner time toward higher-value activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-examination activities that add value (request for comment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Question: What other activities beyond examining (e.g., research or training) could examiners spend time on that would add value? Why do you believe these activities could add value?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invites suggestions for non-production uses of examiner time that would improve quality or value delivered by the USPTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost, pendency, and time tradeoffs (request for comment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Question: Do cost and pendency concerns raise issues that should be considered when determining appropriate examination time?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asks stakeholders to comment on how cost and pendency constraints should influence decisions about examination time allotments and tradeoffs among cost, pendency, and quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public feedback channel and ETA outreach
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO provided ETA website and an email address (ExternalExaminationTimeStudy@USPTO.GOV) for feedback on examination time goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responses to the above questions and participation in roundtables are sought via the ETA website and the provided email; feedback will inform the Agency’s reevaluation of examination time.
